script.opening: (Slow, breathless between short phrases; nasal oxygen tubing visible; pauses to catch his breath.) "That last admission really shook me, doctor. When I can't catch my breath I genuinely think I'm dying — the panic makes it worse. I don't want to end up hooked up to machines in intensive care. But I'm also terrified of suffocating. I suppose I want to talk about what happens from here — if that's alright."

facts.text: Three weeks ago, 9 days in hospital. Had the tight face mask (NIV) for two nights. "Not being able to breathe. Thinking that was it." Third admission this year.
"Breathless even sitting here. Any little thing sets it off, then the panic comes." Needs to rest while washing. When an attack comes: "Put the oxygen up and hope it passes."
"Worried all the time, if I'm honest." Doesn't sleep well, dreads nights. No thoughts of ending his life. Mood low at times but enjoys his grandchildren's visits.

"They're not getting better. I know that." Didn't know NIV (mask) and intubation (tube) are different: "I didn't know the mask was different. The tube, no. The mask — maybe." On CPR, if explained honestly: "Then I wouldn't want it. I'd rather be comfortable."
"Being at home. Not being hooked up to things. And not dying fighting for breath."
Triple inhaler, salbutamol nebuliser, home oxygen 2 L/min 16 hours a day, carbocisteine, a standby rescue pack. No allergies. Has never had morphine: "Morphine? I thought that was for the end."

Lives with his wife, Joan (72), who has arthritis and is tired. Daughter visits most days. Gave up smoking 8 years ago; no one smokes in the house now. Gas hob in the kitchen. Hasn't had a fire-service visit.
No advance care plan, ReSPECT form or lasting power of attorney. Has a will.

Breathless, frightened, thoughtful. Needs short questions and time to answer. If rushed or pushed onto DNACPR too fast, close down: "I'll think about that." Responds to honesty with warmth. Brightens at practical help: "How?" and "If it helps, yes." Ends: "That makes me feel less trapped."

ice.ideas: "I'm getting worse and the treatments aren't working like they did."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror of suffocating and dying in a panic; fear of being kept alive on machines; worried about the strain on Joan.
ice.expectations: "To talk about what happens from here" — and to feel less trapped.

cues: "I genuinely think I'm dying." — the panic cycle to name.
"Hooked up to machines." — explore what he means (tube vs mask).
"Terrified of suffocating." — needs reassurance he won't be left to suffer.

checkpoints.text: Recognises and sensitively initiates ADVANCE CARE PLANNING — exploring his understanding, what matters to him, his fears, and his wishes — at his pace and with permission, prompted by his own opening

Explores the ceiling-of-care/escalation views (hospital vs home, ITU/invasive ventilation, NIV, resuscitation) — clarifying that "no machines" may conflate NIV (often appropriate/reversible) with ITU/CPR — and documents a values-based, revisitable escalation plan (e.g. ReSPECT/DNACPR, shared with ambulance and out-of-hours services — NICE NG142) without coercion, knowing that a legally binding advance decision to refuse life-sustaining treatment must be written, signed, witnessed and state it applies even if life is at risk (Mental Capacity Act 2005)
Names and addresses the BREATHLESSNESS–ANXIETY cycle explicitly, normalising it and giving the patient control strategies

Offers NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL breathlessness management — handheld fan, breathing techniques (pursed-lip/controlled), forward-lean positioning, pacing/energy conservation, psychological/CBT support and a written crisis plan

Knows the PHARMACOLOGICAL options for refractory breathlessness — low-dose opioids (titrated; NICE NG115, dose per BNF) ± benzodiazepine for panic — optimises COPD therapy/oxygen and treats reversible factors, and involves SUPPORTIVE/PALLIATIVE care early (not only for cancer)
Holds honesty and compassion together — validating both fears (machines and suffocation), reassuring he will not be left to suffocate or be abandoned — avoiding false reassurance and bleak fatalism
Paces the conversation to what he wants to discuss today, checks understanding of NIV/ITU/CPR distinctions, and offers to continue over future visits

Safety-nets and follows up: documents and shares the care/escalation plan, arranges symptom-control measures and palliative-care/community involvement, supports any carer, checks home-oxygen fire safety (smoking, naked flames, fire-service visit), gives a crisis plan, and books review — compassionate advance care planning with active symptom control

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you’ve raised this, and it took courage. There’s no rush — we can talk as much or as little today as you want, and come back to it. Can you tell me what frightened you most about that admission?"

"What you describe — not catching your breath, then the panic making it worse — is a real and exhausting cycle, and it’s not weakness. The good news is there’s a lot we can do to break it and give you back some control."

"Let’s be clear about what you don’t want, because ‘machines’ covers different things. Intensive care with a breathing tube — it sounds like that’s not what you’d want, and we can record that. But there’s a gentler mask-based support, used in flares, that can help and is easily stopped — that’s different. Shall we talk through each?"

"Your biggest fear is suffocating — let me reassure you: we have very effective ways to ease the feeling of breathlessness, including small doses of medicine that calm both the breathing sensation and the panic. The aim is that you are comfortable. You will not be left to struggle."

"Some things help straight away — a handheld fan to your face, breathing and positioning techniques, pacing yourself. I’d also like to involve the supportive-care team — they’re not just for the very end; they’re experts in exactly this, and in supporting you and your family."

"I’ll write down your wishes so any doctor who sees you knows them, and we’ll keep reviewing them — nothing is fixed. Who’s at home with you, and who helps you day to day? If someone supports you, let’s make sure they get support too. And with the oxygen — does anyone smoke at home, or are there any open flames? The fire service can do a free safety visit. And we’ll set up a clear plan for what to do in a crisis so you’re never left not knowing."

f.learning: A patient with advanced COPD (MRC dyspnoea 5, home oxygen, recurrent admissions) who, after a frightening admission, raises "what happens from here" is opening the door to ADVANCE CARE PLANNING, and the skill is to seize it sensitively — exploring his understanding, values, fears (suffocation, machines, being a burden) and wishes at his pace and with permission, not as an imposed checklist. Explore the ceiling-of-care/escalation gently: hospital vs home, intensive care/invasive ventilation, NON-INVASIVE ventilation (often appropriate and reversible in exacerbations — clarify, because "no machines" frequently conflates NIV with ITU), and resuscitation status framed around what CPR can realistically achieve in advanced COPD; document a values-based, revisitable escalation plan (e.g. ReSPECT/DNACPR) shared with ambulance and out-of-hours services (NICE NG142), never coerced — and if he wants a legally binding refusal, an advance decision under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 must be written, signed, witnessed and state that it applies even if life is at risk. Centrally, name and address the BREATHLESSNESS–ANXIETY cycle, which amplifies suffering and drives crises: non-pharmacological measures (handheld FAN to the face, pursed-lip/controlled breathing, forward-lean positioning, pacing/energy conservation, CBT-based anxiety support, a written crisis plan) give agency and reduce panic, while for REFRACTORY breathlessness low-dose OPIOIDS (carefully titrated; NICE NG115, dose per BNF) ease the sensation of breathlessness and benzodiazepines can help panic in selected cases — alongside optimised COPD therapy/oxygen and treatment of reversible factors. Involve SUPPORTIVE/PALLIATIVE care early (it is not only for cancer or the final days; NICE NG115: access to palliative and hospice care), support any CARER, and check home-oxygen fire safety (smoking, naked flames; BTS 2015). Communicate with honesty and compassion held together — validate both fears, reassure he will be kept comfortable and not abandoned, clarify NIV/ITU/CPR, avoid both false reassurance and fatalism, pace the discussion and offer to continue.

knowledge.summary: He has opened the door to advance care planning. Explore what matters to him, separate the kinds of “machine”, record his wishes in a shareable plan, and treat the breathlessness-panic cycle actively with non-drug measures, low-dose opioids and palliative-care input.

points.t: Severe COPD with MRC grade 5, home oxygen and repeated admissions is advanced disease with an uncertain but limited prognosis. NICE NG142 [2]: identify people likely to be approaching the end of life and offer advance care planning, with information shared across services.

Explore his understanding, values, fears and wishes at his pace (GMC [4]). Separate the options: hospital admission, non-invasive ventilation (a mask, often used in exacerbations and easy to stop), intubation and intensive care, and CPR. Record the outcome in a ReSPECT plan [3] or local equivalent, and share it with ambulance and out-of-hours services.

Mental Capacity Act 2005 [5]: an advance decision to refuse life-sustaining treatment must be written, signed, witnessed and state that it applies even if life is at risk. He can also appoint a health and welfare lasting power of attorney. A ReSPECT form records recommendations, not a legally binding refusal.

Breathlessness triggers fear, fear speeds breathing, and breathing becomes less efficient. Naming the cycle and giving tools breaks it: handheld fan to the face, pursed-lip and controlled breathing, forward-lean positions, pacing, a written crisis plan, and psychological support.

NICE NG115 [1]: use opioids, when appropriate, to palliate breathlessness in end-stage COPD unresponsive to other medical therapy; benzodiazepines, tricyclic antidepressants, major tranquillisers and oxygen may also be used when appropriate. Start low-dose oral morphine and titrate (dose per BNF [6]); warn about constipation and drowsiness.

NICE NG115 [1]: people with COPD and their families should have access to palliative care services, including hospice care. Involve the community palliative team early, add him to the practice palliative-care register, and offer a carer’s assessment to anyone who supports him.
Review fire risk at every oxygen review: no smoking or naked flames near oxygen, and smoke alarms fitted. NICE NG115 [1] advises a structured risk assessment for home oxygen.

dg.d: Unhurried open start; asked permission and paced the agenda to him.
Home situation and who he wants involved, mood, sleep, and how crises play out at home.
Symptom review, mood screen, record of admissions; bowel and sedation review after starting morphine.
Breathlessness-panic cycle, depression and anxiety, reversible contributors to breathlessness.
Recognised advanced disease; checked for a crisis pattern and mood; no coercion in escalation decisions.
Named advanced COPD honestly and separated ITU, NIV and CPR.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: ReSPECT plan documented and shared; fan, breathing and positioning; low-dose opioid titrated; palliative referral.
Mood and anxiety support, laxative with opioid, oxygen safety, carer’s assessment offered.
Written crisis plan; 999 still available; review call in a week; plan revisitable.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “machines” versus “suffocating” and the panic that drives his crises.
Idea (disease is progressing), concern (suffocation and ITU), expectation (to plan for the future).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror of suffocating and dying in a panic; fear of being kept alive on machines; worried about the strain on Joan — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Albert, I’m Dr Ahmed. Take your time — there’s no rush. What would you like to talk about today?

That last admission really shook me. When I can’t catch my breath I think I’m dying, and the panic makes it worse. I don’t want to end up on machines in intensive care. But I’m terrified of suffocating. I want to talk about what happens from here.

Thank you for raising it. That took courage. We can go as far as you want today and come back to it another time. Would it help to start with what happened in hospital, then talk about your wishes, and then what we can do for the breathlessness and panic?
model.why: Agrees a paced agenda with permission

model.text: Yes. That’s what I want.
What was the most frightening part of that admission?
Not being able to breathe. Thinking that was it.
And now at home, how is your breathing day to day?
Breathless even sitting here. Any little thing sets it off, then the panic comes.
When the panic comes, what do you do?
model.why: Explores current coping and the anxiety cycle

model.text: Put the oxygen up and hope it passes.
How is your mood generally, and your sleep?
Worried all the time, if I’m honest.
Thank you for telling me. Is there someone close to you who you’d want involved in these conversations?
I’ll think about that.
What’s your understanding of where things are with your lungs?
They’re not getting better. I know that.
That’s right, and I’m sorry. What matters most to you from here?
Being at home. Not being hooked up to things. And not dying fighting for breath.

Can I explain the different things people mean by “machines”, so your wishes are clear? One is a breathing tube in intensive care, where you’re put to sleep. Another is a tight mask that helps your breathing during a bad flare, used on a ward, and it can be stopped whenever you want. And then there’s resuscitation if your heart stops.
I didn’t know the mask was different. The tube, no. The mask — maybe.

That’s a really helpful distinction, and you don’t have to decide everything today. About resuscitation: with lungs as damaged as yours, it very rarely works, and it would mean the intensive care you don’t want. How do you feel about that?
Then I wouldn’t want it. I’d rather be comfortable.
Thank you. I’ll write that into a plan called ReSPECT, which ambulance crews and hospital doctors can see. You can change it any time.
model.why: Documents a shareable, revisable escalation plan

model.text: Now your biggest fear, suffocating. I want to be clear: we have good ways to ease breathlessness, and the aim is that you are comfortable. You won’t be left to struggle.
How?

Some things help straight away: a small handheld fan on your face, sitting forward with your arms resting, breathing out slowly through pursed lips. And a very small dose of morphine liquid can ease the feeling of breathlessness itself and calm the panic. At low doses it’s safe and we adjust it carefully.
Morphine? I thought that was for the end.

Many people think that. At this dose it’s used to help breathing for months or years. It can cause constipation and some sleepiness at first, so I’ll give you something for the bowels and we’ll review it within a week.
model.why: Corrects a misconception and explains side effects

model.text: I’d also like to involve the palliative care team. They’re not only for the last days — they’re experts in breathlessness and support people and their families for a long time. And I’ll ask them about talking therapy for the panic.
If it helps, yes.

Let’s write a crisis plan together: fan, position, breathing, your morphine dose, and a number for the palliative team or out-of-hours. If that doesn’t settle things, 999 is still there for you, and the crews will see your plan.
model.why: Crisis plan that respects his wishes

model.text: That makes me feel less trapped.
Can you tell me what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve explained it well?
No tube or resuscitation, maybe the mask, a fan and breathing tricks, a bit of morphine, the palliative team, and a crisis plan.
That’s exactly it. I’ll call you in a week to see how the morphine is going, and we can talk again about anything you’ve thought about.

social.t: Ask who supports him rather than assuming. Offer a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014) and involve people only with his consent.
Low mood and anxiety are common in advanced COPD and worsen breathlessness; screen and offer support.

legal.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: an advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment must be written, signed, witnessed and state it applies even if life is at risk. A health and welfare LPA lets a trusted person decide if he loses capacity.
A ReSPECT plan records recommendations for emergencies. CPR decisions must be discussed with the patient unless this would cause physical or psychological harm (Tracey judgment, 2014).

professional.t: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life: explore wishes, share information honestly at the patient’s pace, and review decisions as things change.
NICE NG142: share the advance care plan with out-of-hours, ambulance and hospital services; add him to the palliative-care register for multidisciplinary review.

community.t: Community palliative care and hospice services, breathlessness services where available, Asthma + Lung UK, and Marie Curie support for non-cancer conditions.

redFlags: Oxygen fire risk (smoking or naked flames near oxygen)
psychosocial: Who he wants involved, and carer strain
What matters most: home, comfort, no intensive care
ice: Concern: suffocating, and being kept alive on machines
Expectation: to talk honestly about what happens next

playbook.diagnosis: “Your COPD is at an advanced stage. It’s unlikely to get better, but there’s a great deal we can do to keep you comfortable and to make sure your wishes are known.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the panic as an alarm that’s set too sensitive. The breathlessness trips it, and the alarm makes the breathing worse. The fan, the positions and a small dose of morphine turn the alarm down.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve told me two fears: machines, and suffocating. We’ve written down what you don’t want, and we’ll make sure you’re not left struggling for breath.”
management.psychosocial: Pace the conversation; involve people only as he chooses; treat mood and panic as part of the plan.
sharedPlan: ReSPECT plan with his wishes on ITU, NIV and CPR, shared with ambulance and out-of-hours
Fan, positions, pursed-lip breathing; low-dose oral morphine with laxative, review within a week
Community palliative care referral; psychological support; carer’s assessment offered
safetyNet: Written crisis plan with palliative and out-of-hours numbers; 999 still available
Review call in a week; plan revisited at every contact

pitfalls.intro: This station is about a conversation, not a form. Candidates fail by rushing to DNACPR, by avoiding the subject, or by leaving the fear of suffocation unanswered.

items.fail: Opening with “Have you thought about resuscitation?”
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s agenda.” He came with fears to be heard first.
items.fix: “What was the most frightening part of that admission?”

items.fail: Treating “no machines” as a refusal of all ventilation.
items.why: NIV is often appropriate and reversible; an unclarified refusal may deny him treatment he would accept.
items.fix: Explain ITU, NIV and CPR separately and record each wish.

items.fail: Offering only more oxygen or another inhaler for the breathlessness.
items.why: NICE NG115 supports opioids and other palliative measures for refractory breathlessness; missing them is a Tasks gap.
items.fix: Fan, positions, breathing, and low-dose morphine with a laxative and review.

items.fail: False reassurance — “you’ve got plenty of time” — or bleak fatalism.
items.why: Both close the conversation; examiners look for honesty with compassion.
items.fix: “Your lungs aren’t getting better, and there’s a lot we can do to keep you comfortable.”

items.fail: Not referring to palliative care because “it isn’t cancer”.
items.why: NICE NG115 says people with COPD should have access to palliative and hospice care.
items.fix: “They’re experts in breathlessness, not only in the last days.”

items.fail: Ending without a crisis plan or a record that others can see.
items.why: His wishes are only protected if ambulance and out-of-hours clinicians know them.
items.fix: ReSPECT plan shared, written crisis plan, review call in a week.

timeMap.d: Thank him for raising it. Agree what to cover today and that it can continue.
The admission, breathlessness now, the panic, what he does in a crisis, mood and sleep, who he wants involved.
What he knows about his lungs, what matters most: home, no tube, not dying breathless.
ITU versus NIV versus CPR; ReSPECT. Fan, positions, breathing, low-dose morphine with laxative, palliative team, talking therapy.
Written crisis plan, teach-back, review call in a week, door left open.

wordPics.fail: Rushes to a DNACPR form or avoids the subject entirely; lumps all “machines” together; offers only more inhalers or oxygen; no plan for the panic; false reassurance or bleak fatalism.
wordPics.pass: Explores his wishes, discusses resuscitation and ventilation, documents a plan, offers non-drug breathlessness measures and considers low-dose opioids, and refers to palliative care.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: paces the conversation to him; separates ITU, NIV and CPR so his choice is informed; addresses the suffocation fear directly; corrects the “morphine means the end” belief; builds a written crisis plan; checks mood; teach-back and a review date.

avoid.dont: “So shall we put a DNR on your notes?”
avoid.instead: “Can I explain the different things people mean by machines, so your wishes are clear?”
avoid.why: A form-first approach feels like withdrawal of care; values come first.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, you’ve got plenty of time.”
avoid.instead: “Your lungs aren’t getting better, and that’s why planning now is so valuable.”
avoid.why: False reassurance blocks the conversation he came to have.

avoid.dont: “There’s nothing more we can do for your breathing.”
avoid.instead: “There’s a lot we can do to make the breathlessness easier and keep you comfortable.”
avoid.why: Palliation is active treatment; fatalism worsens the panic.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: He has opened the door to advance care planning. Explore what matters to him, separate the kinds of “machine”, record his wishes in a shareable plan, and treat the breathlessness-panic cycle actively with non-drug measures, low-dose opioids and palliative-care input.

points.t: Severe COPD with MRC grade 5, home oxygen and repeated admissions is advanced disease with an uncertain but limited prognosis. NICE NG142 [2]: identify people likely to be approaching the end of life and offer advance care planning, with information shared across services.

Explore his understanding, values, fears and wishes at his pace (GMC [4]). Separate the options: hospital admission, non-invasive ventilation (a mask, often used in exacerbations and easy to stop), intubation and intensive care, and CPR. Record the outcome in a ReSPECT plan [3] or local equivalent, and share it with ambulance and out-of-hours services.

Mental Capacity Act 2005 [5]: an advance decision to refuse life-sustaining treatment must be written, signed, witnessed and state that it applies even if life is at risk. He can also appoint a health and welfare lasting power of attorney. A ReSPECT form records recommendations, not a legally binding refusal.

Breathlessness triggers fear, fear speeds breathing, and breathing becomes less efficient. Naming the cycle and giving tools breaks it: handheld fan to the face, pursed-lip and controlled breathing, forward-lean positions, pacing, a written crisis plan, and psychological support.

NICE NG115 [1]: use opioids, when appropriate, to palliate breathlessness in end-stage COPD unresponsive to other medical therapy; benzodiazepines, tricyclic antidepressants, major tranquillisers and oxygen may also be used when appropriate. Start low-dose oral morphine and titrate (dose per BNF [6]); warn about constipation and drowsiness.

NICE NG115 [1]: people with COPD and their families should have access to palliative care services, including hospice care. Involve the community palliative team early, add him to the practice palliative-care register, and offer a carer’s assessment to anyone who supports him.
Review fire risk at every oxygen review: no smoking or naked flames near oxygen, and smoke alarms fitted. NICE NG115 [1] advises a structured risk assessment for home oxygen.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Unhurried open start; asked permission and paced the agenda to him.
Home situation and who he wants involved, mood, sleep, and how crises play out at home.
Picked up “machines” versus “suffocating” and the panic that drives his crises.
Idea (disease is progressing), concern (suffocation and ITU), expectation (to plan for the future).
Symptom review, mood screen, record of admissions; bowel and sedation review after starting morphine.
Breathlessness-panic cycle, depression and anxiety, reversible contributors to breathlessness.
Recognised advanced disease; checked for a crisis pattern and mood; no coercion in escalation decisions.
Named advanced COPD honestly and separated ITU, NIV and CPR.
ReSPECT plan documented and shared; fan, breathing and positioning; low-dose opioid titrated; palliative referral.
Mood and anxiety support, laxative with opioid, oxygen safety, carer’s assessment offered.
Written crisis plan; 999 still available; review call in a week; plan revisitable.

social.t: Ask who supports him rather than assuming. Offer a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014) and involve people only with his consent.
Low mood and anxiety are common in advanced COPD and worsen breathlessness; screen and offer support.

legal.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: an advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment must be written, signed, witnessed and state it applies even if life is at risk. A health and welfare LPA lets a trusted person decide if he loses capacity.
A ReSPECT plan records recommendations for emergencies. CPR decisions must be discussed with the patient unless this would cause physical or psychological harm (Tracey judgment, 2014).

professional.t: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life: explore wishes, share information honestly at the patient’s pace, and review decisions as things change.
NICE NG142: share the advance care plan with out-of-hours, ambulance and hospital services; add him to the palliative-care register for multidisciplinary review.

community.t: Community palliative care and hospice services, breathlessness services where available, Asthma + Lung UK, and Marie Curie support for non-cancer conditions.

redFlags: Oxygen fire risk (smoking or naked flames near oxygen)
psychosocial: Who he wants involved, and carer strain
What matters most: home, comfort, no intensive care
ice: Concern: suffocating, and being kept alive on machines
Expectation: to talk honestly about what happens next

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Your COPD is at an advanced stage. It’s unlikely to get better, but there’s a great deal we can do to keep you comfortable and to make sure your wishes are known.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the panic as an alarm that’s set too sensitive. The breathlessness trips it, and the alarm makes the breathing worse. The fan, the positions and a small dose of morphine turn the alarm down.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve told me two fears: machines, and suffocating. We’ve written down what you don’t want, and we’ll make sure you’re not left struggling for breath.”
management.psychosocial: Pace the conversation; involve people only as he chooses; treat mood and panic as part of the plan.
sharedPlan: ReSPECT plan with his wishes on ITU, NIV and CPR, shared with ambulance and out-of-hours
Fan, positions, pursed-lip breathing; low-dose oral morphine with laxative, review within a week
Community palliative care referral; psychological support; carer’s assessment offered
safetyNet: Written crisis plan with palliative and out-of-hours numbers; 999 still available
Review call in a week; plan revisited at every contact

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is about a conversation, not a form. Candidates fail by rushing to DNACPR, by avoiding the subject, or by leaving the fear of suffocation unanswered.

items.fail: Opening with “Have you thought about resuscitation?”
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s agenda.” He came with fears to be heard first.
items.fix: “What was the most frightening part of that admission?”

items.fail: Treating “no machines” as a refusal of all ventilation.
items.why: NIV is often appropriate and reversible; an unclarified refusal may deny him treatment he would accept.
items.fix: Explain ITU, NIV and CPR separately and record each wish.

items.fail: Offering only more oxygen or another inhaler for the breathlessness.
items.why: NICE NG115 supports opioids and other palliative measures for refractory breathlessness; missing them is a Tasks gap.
items.fix: Fan, positions, breathing, and low-dose morphine with a laxative and review.

items.fail: False reassurance — “you’ve got plenty of time” — or bleak fatalism.
items.why: Both close the conversation; examiners look for honesty with compassion.
items.fix: “Your lungs aren’t getting better, and there’s a lot we can do to keep you comfortable.”

items.fail: Not referring to palliative care because “it isn’t cancer”.
items.why: NICE NG115 says people with COPD should have access to palliative and hospice care.
items.fix: “They’re experts in breathlessness, not only in the last days.”

items.fail: Ending without a crisis plan or a record that others can see.
items.why: His wishes are only protected if ambulance and out-of-hours clinicians know them.
items.fix: ReSPECT plan shared, written crisis plan, review call in a week.
